composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%), produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials. EDS-measured chemistry: Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 (at.%). In the Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu series the Al variation is achieved essentially by substituting Al for Fe (Mn and Cu stay near-constant), and it is Al that governs density (about −0.1 g·cm⁻³ per 1 wt.% Al), giving the 17Al alloy a measured density of 6.76 g·cm⁻³. Design intent: a high Mn level of 35 at.% is used to promote the precipitation kinetics of the ultra-hard β-Mn; Cu was previously shown to accelerate β-Mn precipitation and raise hardness; Al is added both as the primary density-reducing element and as a variable to be explored for its effect on the precipitation and hardening behavior of β-Mn.
conclusions: Within the Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu family, a very wide, flexibly tunable hardness range of 253.4–965.6 HV is obtained through simple aging treatments of no more than 10 h between 525 °C and 650 °C, and the 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C for 6 h contributes the 878.4 ± 28.3 HV plateau of that family. Several family-level trends emerge: (1) increasing Al content slows β-Mn precipitation kinetics and lengthens the time needed for the complete α→β-Mn transformation; (2) increasing Al slightly raises the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn through solid-solution strengthening but also decreases the FCC Cu-rich phase at β-Mn interfaces and reduces the fracture toughness of the ultra-hard alloys; (3) as a combined result, the final hardening effect decreases with increasing Al content. Optimally, the 15Al alloy (Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu) reaches the highest peak hardness of 965.6 HV and a specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g, a level exceeding that of existing low-density steels, other steels and medium/high-entropy alloys (which generally remain below 120 HV·cm³/g). Compared with the 15Al sibling, the 17Al alloy is denser (6.76 g·cm⁻³ vs 6.85 g·cm⁻³ for 15Al), has a lower peak hardness (924.9 HV) and lower fracture toughness, illustrating the hardness–toughness–density trade-off inherent to raising Al. Practically, the low density combined with a wide, adjustable hardness window means these alloys can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to the required hardness, supporting a "one material, multiple uses" strategy and reducing the cost of producing high-hardness, wear-resistant components; the still-modest toughness remains the main limitation to be addressed.
mechanisms: Ultra-high hardness: the α (BCC) matrix → β-Mn transformation is the key to ultra-high hardness, because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (>10 GPa; e.g. 12.2 GPa measured for 17Al). The continuous precipitation of β-Mn during aging therefore turns the soft solution-treated α matrix (~260 HV) into an ultra-hard β-Mn-dominated structure (~900 HV).

Temperature acceleration: increasing the aging temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation and growth, attributed to a larger driving force for β-Mn formation and a higher atomic diffusion rate; consequently at ≥600 °C (including 625 °C) the α→β-Mn transformation of the 17Al alloy is almost complete within just 1 h.

Al slows β-Mn precipitation: increasing Al content decreases the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn through two effects — (i) β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase that must expel Al and Cu as it nucleates and grows, so more Al enriches the surroundings of β-Mn and hinders its further precipitation/growth; and (ii) Al strongly stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase, whose increased amount/size must first be depleted before β-Mn can nucleate and grow, further retarding the transformation.

Solid-solution strengthening of β-Mn by Al: the Al dissolved in β-Mn rises with alloy Al content (15.4→ hmm 14.3 at.% for 15Al, 16.3 at.% for 17Al, 17.5 at.% for 19Al), which slightly enhances the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn through solid-solution strengthening.

Precipitate-induced softening of the overall alloy: as Al content rises, more BCC phase and FCC Cu-rich phase form at the β-Mn interfaces; because their intrinsic hardness is lower than that of β-Mn, they lower the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn and thus reduce the overall microhardness and peak Vickers hardness (e.g. precipitate volume fractions of 3.9 % at 15Al, 4.7 % at 17Al and 6.5 % at 19Al, tracked against falling hardness).

Formation of the BCC interfacial phase: β-Mn growth expels Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the resulting local Al enrichment at the β-Mn interfaces stabilizes the BCC phase that forms there.

Formation of the FCC Cu-rich interfacial phase: because Cu has limited solubility in Fe-based alloys and is expelled from β-Mn during precipitation and growth, Cu concentrates into an FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces, and these particles frequently contain FCC twins.

Fracture-toughness degradation with Al: the K_IC of these ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels decreases with increasing Al content both because the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn rises (making the matrix more brittle) and because the ductile FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces decreases, removing a toughening constituent.
microstructure: After aging at 625 °C for 6 h the α (BCC) matrix of the 17Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn, a Mn-rich phase poor in Al and Cu, with numerous fine BCC and FCC precipitates distributed within the β-Mn. For the 17Al alloy at temperatures ≥600 °C this α→β-Mn transformation is essentially complete within about 1 h of aging, so the 625 °C/6 h state is a fully transformed β-Mn-dominated structure. The fine precipitates sit at β-Mn interfaces: a BCC phase (formed because Al, a BCC stabilizer, is enriched around the β-Mn interfaces as Mn-rich β-Mn expels Al and Cu) and an FCC Cu-rich phase (formed because of the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys and the expulsion of Cu from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth). FCC twins are frequently observed inside these Cu-rich particles. Both precipitates are of comparable particle size. The microstructural evolution sequence followed during aging is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase + α-Mn → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase; the amount of FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content. In the solution-treated precursor state the alloy is single-phase α (BCC).
processing: Alloy ingots were produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick, which were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens by electrical discharge machining for hardness testing and microstructure characterization. Specimens were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq), which yields a single α (BCC) phase. The solution-treated material was then aged at 625 °C for 6 h followed by water quenching; this aging step defines the present sample state. Aging was performed within the broader 525–650 °C / 1–10 h treatment matrix applied to the 15Al, 17Al and 19Al alloys.
properties: Vickers hardness of the 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C for 6 h is 878.4 ± 28.3 HV (HVS-1000 tester, 9.8 N for 15 s, average of 5 measurements; specimen geometry 10 × 5 × 2 mm³). This sits on the near-flat 625 °C plateau of the 17Al alloy (the highest hardness of the 17Al series, 924.9 ± 25.8 HV, occurs after aging at 575 °C for 6 h). Elastic modulus of the 17Al alloy is 175 GPa (from compressive stress-strain curves), and its density is 6.76 g·cm⁻³. Nanoindentation on the hardest 17Al sample gave an average hardness of 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa (Agilent G200, indentation depth 200 nm, points spaced ≥5 µm); because the FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates are softer than β-Mn, the micro-hardness spreads when the indenter contacts them, and the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn (measured on areas free of these precipitates) is 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa, with Al in the β-Mn measured at 16.3 at.%. Characterization techniques applied to the 17Al alloy across the study: Vickers microhardness testing, secondary-electron (SE) SEM imaging (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300; step size 1.5 µm low-magnification / 0.05 µm high-magnification), XRD (D8 Discover), and TEM with SAED and HRTEM plus EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV) on ion-thinned foils. Fracture toughness (indentation technique, K_IC) and comparative peak hardness/fracture toughness versus the 15Al alloy were also evaluated for the family.
summary: This sample is the "17Al" Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel in the state obtained by aging at 625 °C for 6 h followed by water quenching, i.e. one data point in the alloy family Fe-35Mn-(15, 17, 19)Al-5Cu used to map how Al content controls aging hardening. Aging at this temperature (≥600 °C) drives the near-complete α(BCC)→β-Mn transformation within ~1 h, so this condition represents a fully (or nearly fully) β-Mn-transformed, ultra-hard state with a Vickers hardness of 878.4 ± 28.3 HV. It belongs to a study whose central question is whether simple aging treatments can deliver an ultra-wide, flexibly tunable hardness (253.4–965.6 HV) and ultra-high specific hardness in low-density Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels by exploiting the precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase.
unmapped: The reported nanoindentation hardness of 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and the intrinsic β-Mn hardness of 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa belong to the hardest 17Al sample, which is the 575 °C/6 h condition (924.9 HV), not the 625 °C/6 h state of this sample; they are listed here to avoid misattributing them to the 625 °C/6 h condition.

The TEM/SAED/HRTEM characterization of fine β-Mn-interface precipitates for the 17Al alloy was performed on the 575 °C/6 h sample (FCC Cu-rich particles with FCC twins, EDS confirming Cu enrichment with Fe/Mn depletion), rather than on this 625 °C/6 h sample.

The fracture-toughness values (K_IC = 8.6 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 15Al, 6.6 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 17Al, 3.5 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for 19Al) were measured on the peak-hardness samples of the family, not specifically on the 625 °C/6 h state of the 17Al alloy.
